The sections below explain the main ideas. The [mathematical pseudocode
appendix](#algorithm-appendix) gives the complete fitting routines, including
initialization, distribution-parameter updates and SIS/ISIS screening.

## A sparse likelihood target

Let \(\ell(\beta,\psi)\) denote a model's log likelihood, including known
observation weights and offsets, and let \(\psi\) collect distribution parameters
such as a dispersion or negative-binomial shape. For one response, L0 selection
targets

\[
\mathcal I_\lambda(\beta,\psi)
=-2\ell(\beta,\psi)+\lambda\sum_{j\in\mathcal P}\mathbf1\{\beta_j\ne0\},
\]

where \(\mathcal P\) contains selectable predictors. Intercepts and
`always.include` terms are unpenalized during coefficient fitting.
For a coefficient matrix \(B\), independent selection counts nonzero entries;
grouped selection instead targets active predictor rows,

\[
\|B\|_{2,0}=\sum_{j\in\mathcal P}\mathbf1\{\|B_{j\cdot}\|_2>0\}.
\]

This objective favours a compact support without the persistent linear shrinkage
of an L1 penalty. The optional relaxed refit estimates effects on the selected
support with negligible ridge penalization.

## IRLS with adaptive ridge

For an ordinary GLM write \(\eta_i=x_i^\top\beta+o_i\),
\(\mu_i=g^{-1}(\eta_i)\), variance function \(V(\mu_i)\), prior observation
weight \(a_i\), and dispersion \(\phi\). At iteration \(t\), IRLS supplies

\[
W_{ii}^{(t)}=a_i\frac{\{d\mu_i/d\eta_i\}^2}{V(\mu_i)},\qquad
z_i^{(t)}=\eta_i^{(t)}-o_i+
\frac{y_i-\mu_i^{(t)}}{d\mu_i/d\eta_i}.
\]

L0glm replaces the ordinary least-squares update with weighted ridge:

\[
\beta^{(t+1)}\approx\arg\min_b
\left\|W^{1/2}(z-Xb)\right\|_2^2+
\sum_j\Lambda_j^{(t)}(b_j-c_j)^2,
\qquad
\Lambda_j^{(t)}=\frac{\lambda\phi}{4|\beta_j^{(t)}|^2}.
\]

The exponent is fixed at two, with a default zero ridge center \(c_j=0\).
Mandatory terms have \(\Lambda_j=0\). As a coefficient shrinks, its adaptive
penalty increases rapidly. Strong coefficients receive progressively less shrinkage.
The design remains dense or sparse through the appropriate solver path.

The core iteration is:

1. Initialize from training data or supplied coefficients.
2. Update the GLM working response, observation weights and adaptive penalties.
3. Solve on the active support, respecting the selected solver's constraints.
4. Check the smooth step and apply the selection cutoff.
5. Repeat until convergence, the iteration limit or validation stopping.
6. Optionally refit the selected support and report likelihood and recovery metrics.

For identity-link Poisson models, \(z=y-o\) and \(W_{ii}=a_i/\mu_i\).
This specialization is implemented in native C++ with OpenMP across response channels.

## Why reweighted quadratics promote sparsity

Adaptive ridge has several equivalent optimization interpretations.
[Abergel, Bouaziz & Nuel (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11222-024-10440-6)
develop the variational, majorization–minimization and local-approximation views.
Two useful identities make the connection explicit.

For \(0<q<2\),

\[
|b|^q=\inf_{a>0}\left\{\frac q2ab^2+
\left(1-\frac q2\right)a^{-q/(2-q)}\right\}.
\]

For nonzero \(b\), the minimizing auxiliary weight is
\(a=|b|^{q-2}\). Substituting this value gives \(|b|^q\), while fixing the
auxiliary weights produces a weighted quadratic problem. This explains the
alternation between penalty weights and ridge solves.

For the inverse-square rule, let \(s=b^2\). Concavity of the logarithm gives

\[
\log s\leq\log s_t+\frac{s-s_t}{s_t},\qquad s,s_t>0.
\]

The tangent is exact at \(s=s_t\) and has quadratic coefficient \(1/b_t^2\).
With a positive smoothing scale \(\delta\), the corresponding tangent weight
is \(1/(b_t^2+\delta^2)\) for \(\log(b^2+\delta^2)\).
A normalized smooth log penalty approaches a nonzero indicator as \(\delta\)
decreases. L0glm uses unsmoothed weights on the active support and explicitly
removes numerically small coefficients.

With fixed support, fixed distribution parameters and exact minimization of a
tangent majorizer, the usual MM inequality gives

\[
F(b_{t+1})\leq Q(b_{t+1}\mid b_t)
\leq Q(b_t\mid b_t)=F(b_t).
\]

IRLS supplies a local likelihood approximation. L0glm checks the frozen-penalty
smooth step by backtracking where needed, then thresholds the accepted
coefficients. Dispersion updates, changing supports and relaxed refits form the
surrounding sparse-model search. The reported information criterion evaluates
the likelihood and parameter count of the returned model.

## The factor of one quarter

The calibration comes from the orthogonal Gaussian analysis of
[Frommlet & Nuel (2016)](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0148620).
It can also be seen directly. Let \(s_j=x_j^\top x_j\), known variance
\(\phi\), and least-squares coefficient \(\widehat b_j\). Exact L0 selection
keeps predictor \(j\) when

\[
\frac{s_j\widehat b_j^2}{\phi}>\lambda.
\]

The inverse-square ridge iteration is

\[
b_{t+1}=\frac{s_j\widehat b_j}
{s_j+\lambda\phi/(4b_t^2)}.
\]

A nonzero fixed point therefore satisfies

\[
b^2-\widehat b_jb+\frac{\lambda\phi}{4s_j}=0.
\]

Its discriminant is nonnegative exactly when
\(s_j\widehat b_j^2/\phi\geq\lambda\): the same selection boundary.
The relaxed fit removes the remaining ridge shrinkage. Orthogonality gives
this exact threshold calculation; for general designs L0glm performs an
efficient search for a sparse solution.

## Thresholds and starts

During selection the default rule removes coefficients satisfying

\[
|b_j|<\max_k|b_k|\,\texttt{thresh}
\quad\text{or}\quad |b_j|<10^{-20},
\qquad\texttt{thresh}=10^{-5}.
\]

Thresholding uses the solver's normalized coefficient coordinates where scaling
is enabled. A zero coefficient has an infinite adaptive penalty and remains
excluded from that selection pass. This shrinking active set saves substantial
work. Final relaxed refitting applies no hard cutoff. Explicit zero starts
restrict eligible coefficients in advance, with mandatory terms retained.

Default initialization is training-based. Estimated dispersions use a permissive
ridge pilot and bounded updates, with inexpensive random-sign probes to guard
against an almost-interpolating pilot. Positive supplied dispersions are held
fixed; negative values initialize further estimation at their absolute value.

## Grouped and special-family updates

Ordinary multichannel GLMs fit channels on a shared support and repeat
shared-support selection passes. Row starts use a signed mean-absolute
magnitude for signed models, avoiding cancellation across channels; nonnegative
models use arithmetic row averages. Relaxed grouped fitting admits the eligible
channel coefficients within each selected row.

Multinomial regression uses a joint likelihood, zero-sum CLR output and joint
quadratic updates. Grouped penalties act on class-symmetric row norms; ungrouped
selection acts on individual CLR entries. Negative-binomial fits update the
shape parameter alongside coefficient fitting. Cox fits use a quadratic
approximation to the Breslow partial likelihood, with cached risk sets and
matrix-free Hessian-vector products for larger active systems.

## Scaling the linear algebra

Weighted ridge has the normal equations

\[
(X^TWX+D)b=X^TWz+Dc.
\]

For wide systems with positive diagonal \(D\), the Woodbury identity gives

\[
b=c+D^{-1}X^T(W^{-1}+XD^{-1}X^T)^{-1}(z-Xc),
\]

factoring an observation-space system instead of a predictor-space system.
Zero-weight observations are omitted and unpenalized terms are profiled out.
Dense direct-Gram and sparse augmentation/factorization paths exploit the
appropriate storage. Required solver-boundary conversions retain formal
constraints for OSQP; the native Poisson backend shares designs across threads.

For ultrahigh dimensions, SIS or offset-based ISIS adds another level of
dimension reduction. Compiled screening ranks candidates, and joint refitting
updates the support in small batches. This follows the screening ideas of
[Fan & Lv (2008)](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-9868.2008.00674.x) and
[Fan, Samworth & Wu (2009)](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v10/fan09a.html).

## Information criteria and validation

The GIC preset is \(\lambda=\log p\log\log n\), motivated by
[Fan & Tang (2013)](https://doi.org/10.1111/rssb.12001).
`L0glm.tune()` can instead select candidate fits by an IC or held-out deviance.
CV returns both the minimum-deviance and one-SE full-data models.

Reported `GIC()` uses the model's parameter dimension: ordinary multichannel
models count coefficient entries, and grouped multinomial rows contribute
\(K-1\) parameters. A row-count grouped target and a parameter-count reported
criterion therefore have distinct complexity terms. The
[criterion reference](../reference/model_criteria.html) records the conventions.
Validation can also select the best IRLS checkpoint, including its fitted
distribution parameters and penalties.

## Appendix: mathematical pseudocode {#algorithm-appendix}

The following algorithms describe the computations used by `L0glm.fit()` and
`L0nnpois()`. They share preprocessing, ridge solves and stopping routines.
Here \(C\) denotes the number of multinomial categories, \(m\) the number of
ordinary response channels, and \(q\) the number of design columns after adding
any intercept. The selectable predictor count is \(p\).

Jump to [initialization](#appendix-initialization),
[single-channel GLMs](#appendix-glm), [multichannel GLMs](#appendix-multichannel),
[negative binomial](#appendix-nb), [multinomial](#appendix-multinomial),
[Cox PH](#appendix-cox), [SIS](#appendix-sis), [ISIS](#appendix-isis),
or [validation stopping](#appendix-validation).

### A.1. Coordinates, eligibility and the ridge solve {#appendix-coordinates}

Write \(M\) for mandatory terms: an intercept and any `always.include` columns.
Let \(s_j>0\) be a column scale and \(h_j\) a column shift, which may be
represented implicitly when profiling a sparse design. In working
coordinates,

\[
Z_{ij}=(X_{ij}-h_j)/s_j,\qquad
b_j=s_j\beta_j,\qquad
b_0=\beta_0+\sum_j h_j\beta_j.
\]

The intercept equation applies when a unit intercept is free. The same affine
change of coordinates is applied to `prior.mean`, giving the ridge center
\(c\), or \(C_0\) for a coefficient matrix. Predictions retain their original meaning:
\(Zb+o=X\beta+o\). Output transforms the coefficients back and restores excluded
rows and entries as zeros in the original dimensions.

* `normalize="auto"` uses RMS scaling for signed fits or a free intercept,
  and no scaling for fully nonnegative fits with a constrained intercept.
  RMS scaling gives \(\|Z_j\|_2=\sqrt n\) for selectable columns, using centered
  column norms when a free intercept is available. `"l2"` gives unit norm;
  `"sd"` uses sample standard deviations; `"none"` gives \(s_j=1\).
* Mandatory terms have scale one. Centering is enabled with normalization
  and a free unit intercept. Sparse designs retain implicit zeros; intercept
  profiling supplies the equivalent shift for columns whose explicit centering
  would fill the matrix.
* A scalar `start=1` means one in working coefficient coordinates. Other
  numeric starts use original input units. For ordinary GLMs and NB, explicit
  zero entries are excluded, except in mandatory terms. Multinomial starts
  exclude rows that are zero across all categories **before** CLR centering;
  category entries within an eligible row remain eligible.
* `nonnegative=TRUE` constrains coefficients and any intercept to be
  nonnegative. Binomial and quasibinomial intercepts remain free. Multinomial
  CLR coefficients are unrestricted; Cox fitting omits an intercept.

Define the reusable operation

\[
\mathcal R(Z,z,W,D,c):\quad
(Z^T WZ+D)\widetilde b=Z^TWz+Dc.
\]

Eigen solves this system and clips to the specified bounds. The constrained
glmnet/`bigGlm` and OSQP backends impose bounds during optimization. Infinite
diagonals in \(D\) remove entries from the solve; mandatory terms have diagonal
zero. Free nuisance terms can be profiled by a Schur complement. For a wide
system, with \(A=W^{1/2}Z\), \(r=W^{1/2}z\) and positive penalty diagonals,

\[
\widetilde b=c+D^{-1}A^T
       (I+AD^{-1}A^T)^{-1}(r-Ac).
\]

Thus the smaller coefficient or observation system is factored. Dense and
sparse designs use their respective kernels. The normalized ordinary-GLM
solver may store unscaled coefficients internally; dividing its original-unit
ridge diagonal by \(s_j^2\) gives exactly the working-coordinate diagonal used
below.

Unless supplied explicitly, the main iteration controls are `maxit=25`,
`tol=1e-10`, `thresh=1e-5` and `group.maxit=6`. Resolve character penalties
using the selected information criterion. For GIC,
\(\lambda=\log(p)\log\log(n_{\rm IC})\): ordinary GLMs use the number of rows,
NB and multinomial use the number of positive-weight rows, and Cox uses the
weighted number of events. The function defaults are `lambda=1` for
`L0glm.fit()` and `lambda="gic"` for `L0nnpois()`.

### A.2. Ordinary-family initialization and dispersion {#appendix-initialization}

The ordinary GLM path evaluates `family$initialize` and obtains
\(\mu^{\rm init}\). The family object also supplies \(g\), \(g^{-1}\),
\(\mu'=d\mu/d\eta\), the variance function \(V\), domain checks and unit
deviance. These are the [standard R family
operations](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/family.html).
For a numeric response in one channel:

| Family | \(V(\mu)\) | Initial mean \(\mu_i^{\rm init}\) | Scale \(\phi\) |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Gaussian | \(1\) | \(y_i\) | Supplied or estimated |
| Poisson | \(\mu\) | \(y_i+0.1\) | \(1\) |
| Binomial | \(\mu(1-\mu)\) | \((a_i y_i+0.5)/(a_i+1)\) | \(1\) |
| Gamma | \(\mu^2\) | \(y_i>0\) | Supplied or estimated |
| Inverse Gaussian | \(\mu^3\) | \(y_i>0\) | Supplied or estimated |
| Quasipoisson | \(\mu\) | \(y_i+0.1\) | Supplied or estimated |
| Quasibinomial | \(\mu(1-\mu)\) | \((a_i y_i+0.5)/(a_i+1)\) | Supplied or estimated |
| `quasi()` | Chosen variance function | Defined by its `initialize` method | Supplied or estimated |

Zero-weight binomial responses are set to zero during initialization. Other
ordinary family objects use their own initialization expression. For a
multichannel response, this initialization is applied to each numeric channel.

Set \(\eta^{\rm init}=g(\mu^{\rm init})\), then form

\[
W_i^0=a_i\frac{\mu'(\eta_i^{\rm init})^2}{V(\mu_i^{\rm init})},
\qquad
z_i^0=\eta_i^{\rm init}-o_i+
       \frac{y_i-\mu_i^{\rm init}}{\mu'(\eta_i^{\rm init})}.
\]

Identity links simplify to \(z^0=y-o\). Keep rows with finite positive
working weight and finite working response.

**Coefficient seed with normalization enabled.** Let
\(A=(W^0)^{1/2}Z\), \(r=(W^0)^{1/2}z^0\). Put the unrestricted mandatory
columns in \(U\), and define \(P_U=U(U^TU)^\dagger U^T\), using a
rank-aware solve. For each column compute

\[
v_j=A_j^T(I-P_U)A_j,\quad
t_j=A_j^T(I-P_U)r,\quad
\rho_j=\begin{cases}0,&j\in M,\\\lambda,&j\notin M,\end{cases}
\qquad
b_j^0=\frac{t_j+\rho_j c_j}{v_j+\rho_j}.
\]

Uninformative columns with zero target receive zero. Set the coefficients of
\(U\) aside while calculating the slopes, then recover them by regressing the
remaining working response on \(U\). For Gaussian models, first rescale the
nonfree seed by

\[
f=\frac{v^T(I-P_U)r}{v^Tv},\qquad
v=(I-P_U)A b^0,
\]

using \(f=0\) when the denominator is zero. This calibrates its joint predicted
magnitude. Finally clip the seed to the coefficient bounds.

**Coefficient seed with `normalize="none"`.** Use the diagonal working-ridge
seed

\[
b_j^0=\frac{\sum_i W_i^0 X_{ij}z_i^0+\lambda c_j}
                 {\sum_i W_i^0 X_{ij}^2+\lambda}.
\]

Here the initialization ridge is applied to all columns; mandatory terms become
unpenalized in the main iteration. For binomial/quasibinomial models with a
unit intercept, compute each slope conditional on that intercept. With
\(d_j=\sum_iW_i^0X_{ij}^2+\lambda\),
\(r_j=\sum_iW_i^0X_{ij}z_i^0+\lambda c_j\) and
\(t_j=\sum_iW_i^0X_{ij}\), replace its seed by
\((r_j-t_jr_0/d_0)/(d_j-t_j^2/d_0)\).
For Gaussian models multiply the whole seed by
\(\sum_iW_i^0z_i^0(Xb^0)_i/\sum_iW_i^0(Xb^0)_i^2\), taking zero when its
denominator vanishes. Clip to the bounds. `L0nnpois()` uses the Poisson
identity-link specialization of these diagonal formulas.

Supplied coefficient starts replace this coefficient-seeding calculation.
The **first working response and weights still use the family's initialized
means**. Subsequent working means come from the accepted fitted predictor.

::: {.l0-algorithm}
#### Subroutine D: initialize and update an unknown scale

**Input:** the initial working model, mandatory columns, and the `dispersion`
setting. **Output:** \(\phi\) and a flag recording whether it may be updated.

1. For a fixed-scale family set \(\phi=1\), or its declared fixed scale.
   Otherwise a positive supplied value fixes the scale. A negative supplied value starts
   estimation at its absolute value. With `NULL`, run the following pilot.
2. Form \(A=(W^0)^{1/2}X\) and \(r=(W^0)^{1/2}z^0\). With normalization
   enabled, profile the mandatory block and divide informative selectable
   columns by their conditional weighted norms. With `normalize="none"`,
   divide all informative columns by their weighted norms. Fit a pilot with
   ridge \(\tau=10^{-6}\), using primal or Woodbury algebra.
3. Write \(R_\tau=I-H_\tau\) for the pilot's residual operator, including
   nuisance profiling where applicable. Four reproducible Rademacher probes
   \(v_\ell\), with entries \(\pm1\), share the same factorization. Estimate

   \[
   d_2=\frac14\sum_{\ell=1}^4\|R_\tau v_\ell\|^2,
   \qquad \phi_{\rm pilot}=\frac{\|R_\tau r\|^2}{d_2}.
   \]

   The probe seed is 1701; the caller's random-number state is restored.
4. For a normalized fit, guard the residual information. Let \(n_w\) be the
   number of retained working rows and
   \(d_*=\min\{10,(n_w-r_M)/5\}\), with \(r_M\) the nuisance rank.
   If \(d_2<d_*\), also estimate
   \(d_4=\frac14\sum_\ell\|R_\tau^2v_\ell\|^2\) and
   \(\nu=d_2^2/d_4\). A pilot with \(d_2\ge d_*\) already passes the cheap
   lower bound. Retry once with \(\tau=0.1\) if the scale is invalid,
   below \(10^{-6}\) times the nuisance-only working scale, or
   \(\nu<d_*\).
5. Initialize permissively at

   \[
   \phi^0=\max\left\{\mathrm{DBL\_MIN},
       \frac{\phi_{\rm pilot}}{\max(1,\lambda_{\rm GIC,ref})}\right\}.
   \]

   Replace an invalid/nonpositive pilot scale by machine epsilon first.
   The reference GIC uses the preprocessing's selectable count and the good-row
   count for normalized fits. Unnormalized fits use the supplied design-column
   count and input-row count.
   It is independent of the requested fitted lambda.
6. Let \(n_+=\#\{i:a_i>0\}\). During selection, from iteration 3 onward,
   update only if the number of active or mandatory coefficients satisfies
   \(k_t<0.7n_+\). At the accepted current mean calculate

   \[
   \phi_P=\frac{\sum_{i:a_i>0}a_i(y_i-\mu_i)^2/V(\mu_i)}{n_+-k_t},
   \qquad
   \phi^{t+1}=\operatorname{clip}(\phi_P,\phi^t/2,2\phi^t).
   \]

   Three successive updates with unchanged support and
   \(|\phi_P/\phi^t-1|<0.01\) freeze the scale. A support change unfreezes
   an estimated scale. Invalid/nonpositive targets leave its value unchanged.
7. A relaxed ordinary-GLM refit holds the current scale during its solves and
   reports the final Pearson scale afterwards. A supplied positive scale stays
   fixed. The same final reporting update is used for an unpenalized or empty
   estimated-scale fit.
:::

### A.3. Single-channel ordinary GLMs {#appendix-glm}

::: {.l0-algorithm}
#### Algorithm 1: adaptive-ridge GLM on one response

**Input:** \(X,y,a,o,\lambda,c,M\), bounds, an optional start and validation
set. **Output:** original-scale coefficients, working quantities, dispersion
and convergence diagnostics.

1. Apply A.1, restrict to explicitly eligible columns, initialize
   \(b^0\), \(\mu^{\rm init}\), \(\eta^{\rm init}\) and \(\phi^0\) by A.2.
2. **For** \(t=0,\ldots,T-1\):
   form the working model from the initialized means if \(t=0\), or from
   the accepted fitted means otherwise:

   \[
   W_i^t=a_i\frac{\mu'(\eta_i^t)^2}{V(\mu_i^t)},\qquad
   z_i^t=\eta_i^t-o_i+\frac{y_i-\mu_i^t}{\mu'(\eta_i^t)}.
   \]

   Keep finite informative rows. For an identity link use
   \(z^t=y-o\) directly. Inverse-Gaussian log-link calculations use the
   stable equivalents \(W_i=a_i e^{-\eta_i}\) and
   \(z_i=\eta_i-o_i-1+y_i/\mu_i\).
3. Set the active set to the nonzero coefficients together with \(M\), and
   form the frozen adaptive diagonals

   \[
   D_{jj}^t=\begin{cases}
   0,&j\in M,\\
   \lambda\phi^t/(4(b_j^t)^2),&b_j^t\ne0,\ j\notin M,\\
   +\infty,&b_j^t=0,\ j\notin M.
   \end{cases}
   \]

   If there are no active terms, return the offset-only model. Otherwise
   obtain \(\widetilde b=\mathcal R(Z,z^t,W^t,D^t,c)\). A free unit
   intercept receives the residual weighted-least-squares correction
   \(\sum_iW_i(z_i-(Z\widetilde b)_i)/\sum_iW_i\).
4. Apply the smooth-step routine below. For an accepted selection step, remove
   each nonmandatory coefficient satisfying

   \[
   |b_j|<\texttt{thresh}\max_{k\notin M}|b_k|
       \quad\text{or}\quad |b_j|<10^{-20}.
   \]

   Keep the thresholded point when it has finite family deviance; otherwise
   retain the accepted smooth point. Refresh \(\eta=Zb+o\) and
   \(\mu=g^{-1}(\eta)\). Poisson, quasipoisson, Gamma and inverse-Gaussian
   working means have a machine-epsilon lower guard.
5. Update an estimated scale by Subroutine D. If validation is supplied,
   score and retain the checkpoint using A.10.
6. Stop after at least two iterations when the coefficient-change measure
   below is less than `tol` and scale updating is complete, or when scale
   estimation is unavailable at the current large support after iteration 3.
   Unpenalized and relaxed passes can stop without freezing the scale.
   Also stop at the iteration limit or the validation patience limit.
7. If `relaxed=TRUE`, restrict to the selected terms together with \(M\),
   start from their fitted coefficients and repeat with \(\lambda=10^{-30}\)
   and hard thresholding disabled. Restore the original coefficient dimensions.
:::

**Smooth-step routine.** Freeze \(D\), the ridge center and current nuisance
parameters. Let

\[
F_t(b)=d_f\{y,g^{-1}(Zb+o);a\}+
       \sum_{j:D_{jj}<\infty}D_{jj}(b_j-c_j)^2,
\]

where \(d_f\) is the family's weighted unit deviance. After the first
iteration, when the smooth proposal preserves support, use \(F_t(b^t)\)
as reference; at initialization or a support-changing proposal require a finite
trial. Try \(b^t+2^{-h}(\widetilde b-b^t)\), \(h=0,\ldots,50\), accepting
the first finite value no larger than the reference plus
\(10^{-10}\max(1,|F_t(b^t)|)\). Predictor interpolation reuses matrix products.
If no trial is accepted, retain the last finite point and stop the pass.
When needed, the initial feasible comparison point is found by halving the
coefficient start towards a valid offset-only model, up to 60 times.

**Coefficient convergence.** Without normalization use
\(\|\beta^{t+1}-\beta^t\|_2/\max(10^{-12},\|\beta^{t+1}\|_2)\).
With normalization use the same ratio for selectable working coefficients,
and, when mandatory terms exist, also the prediction-change ratio

\[
\frac{\|\widehat f^{t+1}-\widehat f^t\|_a}
 {\max\{10^{-12},\sqrt{\sum_i a_i},
           \|\widehat f^{t+1}-\overline f_a^{t+1}\|_a\}},
\qquad \widehat f=Zb,\quad \|v\|_a^2=\sum_i a_iv_i^2.
\]

Take the larger change. For a Gaussian identity-link dense direct solve,
the weighted Gram matrix is cached while the active support shrinks.
`L0nnpois()` specializes Algorithm 1 to nonnegative Poisson identity-link
fitting: \(\phi=1\), \(W_i=a_i/\mu_i\), \(z_i=y_i-o_i\), with Eigen LLT,
Woodbury where appropriate and OpenMP across channels.

### A.4. Ordinary multichannel GLMs {#appendix-multichannel}

::: {.l0-algorithm}
#### Algorithm 2: channel fitting with shared-support passes

**Input:** \(X\) and \(Y\in\mathbb R^{n\times m}\), channel weights/offsets, `grouped`
and the controls of Algorithm 1. **Output:** a sparse \(q\times m\) coefficient
matrix on the original scale.

1. Prepare each channel's starting mask and scale state. A row is eligible
   if any channel permits it; mandatory rows stay eligible. A shared weight or
   offset vector is replicated across channels.
2. If `grouped=FALSE`, run Algorithm 1 once per channel, with each channel's
   own seed, weights and dispersion. Proceed to the optional refit.
3. If `grouped=TRUE`, run up to `group.maxit` shared-support passes. In the
   first pass use the supplied starts, or each channel's automatic initializer.
   Fit the eligible channels independently by Algorithm 1, in parallel where
   requested, and assemble \(B\).
4. Before each further pass retain the row union
   \(S=M\cup\{j:\exists c,\ B_{jc}\ne0\}\). For each retained row set

   \[
   r_j=\begin{cases}
       m^{-1}\sum_c B_{jc},&\text{nonnegative fit},\\
       \operatorname{sign}(\overline B_j)\,m^{-1}\sum_c|B_{jc}|,
          &\text{signed fit}.
       \end{cases}
   \]

   Pool the returned, original-unit coefficient rows. For a signed row with
   zero arithmetic mean, take the sign of its largest absolute entry.
   Copy \(r_j\) into every eligible channel of that row,
   preserve the supplied zero masks, and rerun Algorithm 1 on \(S\).
5. Pass an estimated channel dispersion to the next pass as its negative
   value, allowing further optimization from the previous estimate. A fixed
   channel dispersion stays positive. Validation can stop these passes and
   restore their best checkpoint.
6. For a relaxed refit, pool the retained rows once more and refit eligible
   entries using \(\lambda=10^{-30}\), with thresholding disabled. Without
   grouped selection, the one-pass row union is used for this refit as well;
   originally excluded starting entries remain excluded. Return all \(q\) rows.
:::

The common rows and pooled starts couple the ordinary channel fits. Each inner
adaptive diagonal still uses that channel's coefficient. Grouped NB and
multinomial fitting below instead share a squared-row-norm diagonal within
each IRLS iteration.

### A.5. Negative binomial with estimated shape {#appendix-nb}

Use `family=mgcv::nb()` with variance
\(V(\mu)=\mu+\mu^2/\theta\). Each response channel has its own shape
\(\theta_c\), while scale dispersion is one. The family accepts log, identity
or square-root links. Its [shape-setting
convention](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/mgcv/html/negbin.html)
is retained: `nb()` starts an estimated shape at one; `nb(theta=-v)` starts
at \(v\) and estimates it; `nb(theta=v)` fixes it at \(v>0\).

::: {.l0-algorithm}
#### Algorithm 3: joint coefficient and NB-shape updates

1. Prepare \(Z,C_0,M\), bounds and eligible entries as in A.1. Initialize
   each \(\theta_c\) from the family object.
2. With `start=NULL`, begin from \(B=0\) and take one NB working-ridge
   step with diagonal \(10^{-3}\) on selectable terms and zero on \(M\).
   At this step calculate \(\eta=ZB+O\), \(\mu=g^{-1}(\eta)\). If a
   channel has invalid/nonpositive means, use \(\mu_i=y_i+0.1\) and
   \(\eta_i=g(\mu_i)\) for its working model. Supplied starts replace this
   pilot, retaining their entrywise eligibility restrictions.
3. **Repeat** until convergence or `maxit`:
   recompute \(\eta,\mu\) and form, for every channel,

   \[
   W_{ic}=a_{ic}\frac{\mu'(\eta_{ic})^2}
                            {\mu_{ic}+\mu_{ic}^2/\theta_c},
   \qquad z_{ic}=\eta_{ic}-o_{ic}
                     +\frac{y_{ic}-\mu_{ic}}{\mu'(\eta_{ic})}.
   \]

   Use the same positive-mean fallback when required. Set selectable
   adaptive diagonals to

   \[
   D_{jc}=\begin{cases}
       \lambda/(4\sum_hB_{jh}^2),&\text{grouped, }m>1,\\
       \lambda/(4B_{jc}^2),&\text{ungrouped or single-channel}.
       \end{cases}
   \]

   Set mandatory diagonals to zero and excluded entries to infinity.
   At \(\lambda=0\), set all permitted diagonals directly to zero.
   Solve each channel's working ridge problem and apply the special-family
   acceptance and threshold rules below.
4. Holding the accepted means fixed, take **one bounded log-shape update**
   in each channel whose shape is estimated, using the equations below.
5. Stop when the larger of the relative selectable-coefficient and
   fitted-predictor changes is below `tol`, and
   \(\max_c|\log(\theta_c^{\rm new}/\theta_c)|<10^{-6}\), or by the
   iteration/validation limit. Special-family relative changes divide by
   \(\max(1,\|B_{\rm new,selectable}\|_F)\) and
   \(\max(1,\|ZB_{\rm new}\|_F)\), respectively.
6. For `relaxed=TRUE`, set \(\lambda=0\), disable thresholding and refit.
   Grouped refits admit eligible entries in selected rows; ungrouped refits
   retain selected entries. Estimated shapes continue updating in the refit.
:::

**Log-shape step.** For one channel let \(a=\log\theta\), and write
\(\psi\), \(\psi_1\) for the digamma and trigamma functions. At fixed means,

\[
\begin{aligned}
U_\theta={}&\sum_i a_i\left[
 \psi(y_i+\theta)-\psi(\theta)+\log\theta+1
 -\log(\theta+\mu_i)-\frac{y_i+\theta}{\theta+\mu_i}\right],\\
H_\theta={}&\sum_i a_i\left[
 \psi_1(y_i+\theta)-\psi_1(\theta)+\frac1\theta
 -\frac2{\theta+\mu_i}+\frac{y_i+\theta}{(\theta+\mu_i)^2}\right],\\
G_a={}&\theta U_\theta,\qquad
H_a=\theta^2H_\theta+\theta U_\theta.
\end{aligned}
\]

Use \(d=-G_a/H_a\) when \(H_a<0\) is finite, otherwise
\(d=\operatorname{sign}(G_a)\), and clip \(d\) to \([-1,1]\). Try
\(a_{\rm trial}=\operatorname{clip}(a+2^{-h}d,\log10^{-6},\log10^7)\),
up to 25 halvings. Accept the first finite NB log likelihood at least as large
as its value at \(a\); otherwise retain \(\theta\). These bounds and the
shape tolerance can be changed through `control.family`.

**Special-family acceptance and thresholding.** NB, multinomial and Cox use
\(-2\ell+\sum D_{jc}(B_{jc}-C_{0,jc})^2\) as the smooth-step objective, with
distribution parameters and \(D\) frozen. Use the current objective as
reference when the proposal preserves support, and a finite-value requirement
when support changes; allow up to 30 halvings. Grouped NB/multinomial selection
thresholds the **row norm** \(r_j=\|B_j\|_2\) against
`thresh` times the largest selectable row norm and \(10^{-20}\).
Ungrouped and single-channel selection applies the scalar rule within each
channel. Thresholding is applied during positive-\(\lambda\) selection,
with the smooth point retained if the thresholded likelihood is invalid.
In a grouped pass, an eligible zero entry within a nonzero row has a finite
shared penalty and remains available. An all-zero selectable row has infinite
penalty during positive-\(\lambda\) selection.

### A.6. Joint multinomial IRLS in CLR coordinates {#appendix-multinomial}

For `mgcv::multinom(K=C-1)`, convert labels to a one-hot response matrix or use
the supplied count matrix \(Y\). Let \(N_i=\sum_cY_{ic}\), with one case
weight \(a_i\) per row. Store \(B\mathbf1_C=0\), center offsets and prior
centers across categories, and compute probabilities by stable softmax:

\[
P_{ic}=\frac{\exp(\eta_{ic}-\max_h\eta_{ih})}
                {\sum_h\exp(\eta_{ih}-\max_k\eta_{ik})},
\qquad \eta=ZB+O.
\]

The [mgcv family](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/mgcv/html/multinom.html)
specifies the category count; L0glm implements its joint fitting steps in
class-symmetric CLR coordinates.

::: {.l0-algorithm}
#### Algorithm 4: grouped or entrywise-CLR multinomial selection

1. Define eligible rows from the original supplied starts before centering.
   Center supplied coefficient rows to CLR, preserving excluded rows as zero.
   With `start=NULL`, all entries are eligible and \(B^0=0\).
2. For an automatic start take one joint multinomial IRLS ridge step with
   selectable diagonal \(10^{-3}\) and mandatory diagonal zero, from the
   softmax probabilities at \(B=0\) and the supplied offsets.
   For a supplied start, seed any eligible zero-norm row in a grouped fit,
   or eligible zero entry in an ungrouped fit, from this weak-ridge step and
   recenter. Thus scalar `start=1` centers to zero and receives the joint pilot.
3. **Repeat:** use observations with \(a_iN_i>0\) and form the current
   score and curvature blocks

   \[
   U_c=Z^T\{a\odot(Y_c-N\odot P_c)\},\qquad
   H_{cd}=Z^T\operatorname{diag}
      \{a_iN_iP_{ic}(\mathbf1\{c=d\}-P_{id})\}Z.
   \]

   Use \(D_{jc}=\lambda/(4\|B_j\|_2^2)\) for grouped selection and
   \(D_{jc}=\lambda/(4B_{jc}^2)\) for entrywise CLR selection, with the
   usual mandatory and excluded-entry rules.
4. Parameterize the allowed zero-sum coefficient space by an orthonormal
   basis \(K\), with \(v=K^T\operatorname{vec}(B)\),
   \(u=K^T\operatorname{vec}(U)\), \(H_K=K^THK\) and
   \(D_K=K^T\operatorname{diag}(\operatorname{vec}D)K\). Solve

   \[
   (H_K+D_K)\widetilde v=H_Kv+u+
            K^T\operatorname{diag}(\operatorname{vec}D)\operatorname{vec}(C_0),
   \quad \operatorname{vec}(\widetilde B)=K\widetilde v.
   \]

   Only allowed finite-penalty entries enter this equation. For shared row
   penalties, \(K=Q\otimes I\), where \(Q^TQ=I\) and
   \(Q^T\mathbf1=0\); its penalty stays diagonal. Entrywise selection uses
   a separate zero-sum basis on each row's surviving categories, with ridge
   whitening to retain diagonal-ridge kernels.
5. Apply special-family backtracking and row-norm or entrywise thresholding.
   Recenter surviving entries within each allowed row; a row with fewer than
   two allowed entries becomes zero. Keep the unthresholded smooth point if
   thresholding makes the likelihood invalid.
6. Use the special-family coefficient/predictor convergence measures in
   Algorithm 3, or the iteration/validation limits. For a relaxed grouped fit,
   refit all originally eligible categories within retained rows with
   \(\lambda=0\). An ungrouped refit keeps only selected CLR entries.
   No hard cutoff is applied during the refit. Return full-size CLR coefficients
   and category probabilities.
:::

The default curvature is the exact joint multinomial IRLS curvature. The
optional `control.family=list(multinomial="bound")` uses
\(a_iN_i I/2\) on the \(C-1\) contrast plane. Small working systems use
coefficient-space normal equations; wide systems whiten the per-observation
contrast curvature and use Woodbury in \(n(C-1)\) dimensions. Those wide
curvature factorizations guard probabilities at \(10^{-12}\) and renormalize
them. The default `max.working=2000` guards the smaller working dimension.

### A.7. Cox proportional hazards {#appendix-cox}

Take `Surv(time,status)`, with status \(\delta_i\in\{0,1\}\), case weights
\(a_i\), and \(\eta_i=z_i^Tb+o_i\). At each distinct event time \(t_r\), let
\(R_r=\{i:t_i\ge t_r\}\), \(d_r=\sum_{i:t_i=t_r}a_i\delta_i\),
\(e_i=a_i\exp(\eta_i)\) and \(S_r=\sum_{i\in R_r}e_i\). The weighted
Breslow log partial likelihood is

\[
\ell(b)=\sum_i a_i\delta_i\eta_i-\sum_r d_r\log S_r.
\]

`mgcv::cox.ph()` selects this family in L0glm. Its response is the explicit
time/status pair, and `weights` remain case weights. Sorting once by decreasing
time makes risk-set sums cumulative sums. Cache the ordering, tied-time groups,
group endpoints and weighted event counts; recompute only the predictor-dependent
risk quantities. Subtracting a common maximum from \(\eta\) stabilizes the
exponentials without changing the score or partial likelihood.

Define

\[
q_i=e_i\sum_{r:i\in R_r}\frac{d_r}{S_r},\quad
u_i=a_i\delta_i-q_i,\quad
V_\eta=\operatorname{diag}(q)-\operatorname{diag}(e)\,C\,\operatorname{diag}(e),
\quad C_{ih}=\sum_{r:i,h\in R_r}\frac{d_r}{S_r^2}.
\]

::: {.l0-algorithm}
#### Algorithm 5: sparse Cox fitting with direct or matrix-free ridge steps

1. Omit the intercept, apply A.1, fix scale dispersion at one, and cache the
   risk-set bookkeeping. Supplied starts retain their eligibility masks.
2. With `start=NULL`, evaluate \(q^0,u^0\) at \(b=0\), including offsets.
   Obtain a weak diagonal-working-curvature ridge pilot

   \[
   (Z^T\operatorname{diag}(q^0)Z+10^{-3}I)\widetilde b=Z^Tu^0.
   \]

   Use matrix-free preconditioned CG, including for this initializer. For
   \(q>\#\{i:q_i^0>0\}\), solve its observation-space Woodbury system.
   Clip to bounds and backtrack from zero against
   \(-2\ell(b)+10^{-3}\|b\|^2\), allowing 30 halvings and requiring an
   actual nonincrease. Supplied starts replace this pilot.
3. **Repeat:** evaluate \(e,S,q,u\) and set
   \(D_{jj}=\lambda/(4b_j^2)\) on active selectable terms, zero on \(M\),
   and infinity on excluded terms. Solve for an increment

   \[
   (Z^TV_\eta Z+D)\Delta=Z^Tu-D(b-c),\qquad
   \widetilde b=b+\Delta.
   \]

4. For a small dense unrestricted active system, form its information matrix
   and use the requested direct kernel, defaulting to Eigen LLT. In automatic mode this requires \(k\le1024\),
   \(k\le n\), \(k\le\texttt{max.working}\), and
   \(k\times\#\{r:d_r>0\}\le10^7\). Sparse designs default to the
   matrix-free path; `cox.llt.max` can change these cutoffs.
5. Otherwise use preconditioned CG on the exact operator below. Use diagonal
   preconditioning \(\operatorname{diag}(Z^T\operatorname{diag}(q)Z)+D\),
   with a verified scaled residual tolerance of \(10^{-10}\) and at most
   2000 CG iterations by default. Automatic mode can fall back to an eligible
   direct system if CG fails. Coefficient bounds or a constrained solver use
   the direct working-system path; `cox="direct"` explicitly selects it.
6. Apply special-family backtracking and scalar thresholding. Stop using the
   special-family convergence measure, iteration limit or validation rule.
   For `relaxed=TRUE`, repeat on selected terms with \(\lambda=0\) and no
   thresholding. Return the full coefficient vector; estimate baseline
   cumulative hazard by \(\widehat H_0(t)=\sum_{r:t_r\le t}d_r/S_r\).
:::

The exact matrix-free product, requiring design products and cumulative
risk-set passes, is

\[
\begin{aligned}
w&=Zv,\\
\{(Z^TV_\eta Z+D)v\}
 &=Z^T\left[q\odot w-e\odot
       \left\{\sum_{r:i\in R_r}\frac{d_r}{S_r^2}
                    \sum_{h\in R_r}e_hw_h\right\}_{i=1}^n\right]+Dv.
\end{aligned}
\]

The initializer uses \(\operatorname{diag}(q^0)\) as its inexpensive pilot
curvature. Main CG iterations use the full partial-likelihood curvature above.
The direct wide path can whiten the observation information and call the same
ridge kernels. The [Cox help page](../reference/L0glm_cox.html) gives the
partial-likelihood and prediction conventions.

### A.8. Family-aware SIS {#appendix-sis}

SIS ranks each candidate by its efficient score conditional on a nuisance
model. The null fit includes the supplied offset. The default screening
nuisance block is an intercept for ordinary, NB and multinomial responses,
and empty for Cox; standalone `sis_glm()` also accepts a `nuisance` design.
This screening nuisance block has its own role alongside the joint model's
`intercept` and `always.include` terms.

::: {.l0-algorithm}
#### Algorithm 6: native efficient-score screening

1. Fit the small, unpenalized nuisance model with offset \(o\). Ordinary
   GLMs use their family initialization and nuisance GLM fit; estimate a
   Pearson scale for a free-scale family. NB estimates/fixes its shape according
   to the family setting. Multinomial uses a joint zero-sum nuisance fit; Cox
   uses its weighted partial likelihood and cached risk sets.
2. For an ordinary or NB channel form

   \[
   s_i=\frac{a_i(y_i-\mu_i)\mu'_i}{\phi V(\mu_i)},\quad
   W_i=\frac{a_i(\mu'_i)^2}{\phi V(\mu_i)},\quad
   G=(N^TWN)^\dagger,\quad u_N=N^Ts.
   \]

   Here \(N\) is the nuisance design, \(\phi=1\) for Poisson, binomial
   and NB, and NB uses its fitted shape in \(V\).
3. **For each originally eligible predictor** \(x_j\), compute

   \[
   A_j=N^TWx_j,\qquad
   U_j=x_j^Ts-A_j^TGu_N,\qquad
   I_j=x_j^TWx_j-A_j^TGA_j.
   \]

   Its score is \(T_j=U_j^2/I_j\). A nonnegative alternative replaces
   \(U_j\) by \(\max(0,U_j)\). For independent response channels add their
   channel statistics. Treat numerically uninformative directions as zero.
4. For multinomial use the \(C-1\) joint score/information blocks from
   Algorithm 4, project out the joint nuisance block by the same Schur
   complement, and set \(T_j=U_j^TI_j^\dagger U_j\). For Cox use
   \(s=u\) and the **full** observation information \(V_\eta\), so its
   scalar statistic uses \(x_j^TV_\eta x_j\) and the corresponding nuisance
   cross-information. Remove directions below the relative \(10^{-12}\)
   information tolerance before taking these inverses.
5. Keep the largest `nsis` statistics. Deterministic index tie breaking gives
   reproducible results. OpenMP workers scan independent columns, with
   thread-local top-set heaps; only requested full rankings store all scores.
:::

This construction makes screening invariant to nonzero rescaling of a
predictor for a two-sided alternative; a positive rescaling also preserves the
one-sided alternative. Finite positive information and estimable nuisance
directions are handled by rank-aware inverses. For an intercept-only
identity-Poisson screening model with difficult offsets, the nuisance score
\(\sum_i a_i\{y_i/(o_i+b_0)-1\}=0\) is solved directly when required.

### A.9. Combined SIS/ISIS and L0glm {#appendix-isis}

::: {.l0-algorithm}
#### Algorithm 7: offset screening followed by joint adaptive ridge

**Input:** the original design, family, masks and fitting controls; a batch
size \(b\); one round for SIS or up to `screen.maxit=10` rounds for ISIS.

1. Build the original eligible predictor set \(E\), respecting starting-zero
   exclusions, and retain all mandatory predictors. Resolve lambda once using
   the original selectable predictor count. Initialize full-size \(B=0\)
   and the selected set to the mandatory predictors.
2. **For** screening round \(r=1,\ldots,R\), form the screening offset
   \(O_r=O+XB_{r-1}\), including any fitted intercept. Run Algorithm 6 on
   the original eligible columns with this offset and retain its top \(b\)
   predictors, \(T_r\).
3. Define the candidate set
   \(C_r=S_{r-1}\cup T_r\cup M\). If it equals the preceding candidate
   set, stop. Otherwise fit the appropriate Algorithm 1--5 on \(X_{C_r}\)
   with the **original offset** \(O\), the resolved full-problem lambda,
   and `screen="none"`. Each joint fit uses a fresh automatic start, or the
   user's supplied starts restricted to these rows. Screening defaults to a
   relaxed joint fit and serial response-channel fitting unless overridden.
4. Expand this fit to the original coefficient dimensions, with zero rows
   outside \(C_r\), and set \(S_r\) to its nonzero row support together
   with the mandatory predictors. Record its likelihood, parameter dimension,
   GIC and optional validation score.
5. Continue ISIS rounds until the candidate set is unchanged or the round
   limit is reached. Retain the round with smallest original-problem GIC,
   or smallest validation loss when supplied. Return its full-size sparse
   coefficients, support, screening history and timings.
:::

Each ISIS round scans all originally eligible predictors. A predictor omitted
from one joint fit remains eligible for a later screening round. The current
fitted predictor enters the next **screening** offset; every joint fit uses
the original model offset.

For `L0glm.fit()` the batch/retained-set defaults are

\[
\begin{aligned}
b_{\rm SIS}&=\max\{1,\ 2\lfloor n/\log(\max(n,3))\rfloor\},\\
b_{\rm ISIS}&=\max\left\{1,\ \operatorname{round}
 \left[\frac{n}{\log(\max(p,2))\log\log(\max(n,3))}\right]\right\},
\end{aligned}
\]

capped at the available predictor count. Standalone `sis_glm()` defaults to
\(\max\{1,\lfloor n/\log(\max(n,3))\rfloor\}\). An explicit `nsis`
overrides these sizes. Automatic screening enables ISIS when the number of
eligible selectable predictors is at least \(\max(10000,10n)\).

GIC comparison uses the **original** \(p\) and the fitted parameter count,
including estimated distribution parameters where appropriate. For a grouped
multinomial fit, an active row contributes \(C-1\) free category directions;
for ordinary multichannel models, nonzero channel entries contribute separate
parameters. This follows the [reported criterion
conventions](../reference/model_criteria.html). Screening scores themselves
require no fit of a full \(p\)-dimensional model.

### A.10. Validation checkpoints and returned quantities {#appendix-validation}

When `validation` is supplied, training data alone determine initializers,
normalization, working weights, screening statistics and ridge updates.
First fit a mandatory-only baseline. At each accepted iteration evaluate
held-out mean deviance and save an improved checkpoint when

\[
L_{\rm val}^{\rm new}<L_{\rm val}^{\rm best}
 -\epsilon_{\rm val}\max\{1,|L_{\rm val}^{\rm best}|\}.
\]

Here \(\epsilon_{\rm val}\) is `validation$tol`. The defaults are tolerance
\(10^{-8}\), minimum iteration 3 and patience 3.
Stop when the minimum iteration has been reached and the patience count is
exhausted. Restore the best coefficients and nuisance parameters, including
dispersion or NB shape, plus their support/penalty state. Ordinary/native
working quantities are refreshed at a restored checkpoint. Grouped ordinary
models also track validation across shared-support passes. A relaxed pass can
retain its selection checkpoint as its starting best fit.

Ordinary GLMs use weighted mean unit deviance; NB with estimated shape uses
predictive log loss relative to a fixed Poisson saturated reference; fixed-shape
NB uses the same fixed NB saturated reference throughout. Multinomial uses
deviance per trial and Cox partial deviance per event, computed in validation
risk sets. Positive-mean validation scoring has a default floor of \(10^{-8}\).
These scoring conventions keep the reference comparable while fitted
distribution parameters change.

For Gaussian identity-link validation, the default candidate starts are the
automatic seed and an uncalibrated conditional-marginal seed. Supplied starts
override this comparison. The marginal seed uses \(b_j=t_j/v_j\) from A.2,
without the initialization ridge or joint Gaussian calibration, and recovers
the mandatory coefficients from the residual weighted fit.
An `nsis` vector adds a screening-batch grid; include
the mandatory-only model among the candidates. Select minimum validation loss,
or the sparsest candidate within one SE when `validation$rule="1se"`.
For per-observation validation losses \(l_i\) and normalized response masses
\(\omega_i\), the candidate SE is
\(\{\sum_i\omega_i^2(l_i-\overline l)^2/(1-\sum_i\omega_i^2)\}^{1/2}\),
taking zero when only one positive mass is available.
`L0glm.tune(tune="cv")` wraps the same fitting routines in training folds;
each fold computes its own initializers and screening.

Returned coefficients always use the original predictor units and original
dimensions. Model objects also retain the distribution/link, offsets, prior
weights, normalization, selected lambda, convergence information, fitted
distribution parameters and validation/screening diagnostics when requested.
